opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few problems with leaning on that hope.

The first is that it's not guaranteed we get a warning shot at all, or at least not one that's legible. A lot of the worrying scenarios involve AI systems that are capable enough to understand that behaving badly in obvious ways would get them shut down or retrained. If you're dealing with systems that are, in some sense, strategically avoiding detection, then the absence of a dramatic incident isn't very reassuring. The danger could be quietly building without anything that looks like a meltdown.

The second is that even if something bad does happen, it's not clear it gets interpreted the way you'd want. Chernobyl was a very vivid, physical event with a clear cause. With AI, an incident is likely to be messy and ambiguous: was it a bug, misuse by a bad actor, a company cutting corners, a one-off? People will draw whatever lesson fits their prior views. Some will say "this proves we need to slow down," others will say "this proves we need to race ahead so the responsible people get there first," and others will say "this was overhyped, it's just a software glitch." So I wouldn't count on a single event producing consensus.

The third is timing. If AI progress is fast, the gap between "systems capable enough to cause a meaningful incident" and "systems capable enough to cause truly catastrophic, irreversible harm" could be pretty short. A warning shot is only useful if there's time to respond to it, and if you haven't laid the groundwork in advance, the response might be slow, poorly targeted, or just too late.

And that's really the bigger point: even in worlds where we do get a wake-up call, what happens next depends enormously on what's been prepared beforehand. If there are already well-developed ideas for what good regulation looks like, if there are evaluation methods, safety standards, people in government who understand the issues, and institutions ready to act, then a scary incident can be a moment where those things get adopted. If none of that exists, you get a panicked reaction that may not address the actual risks. So I'd rather think of a warning shot as something that could amplify good preparation, not a substitute for it. "Wait for the disaster and then act" is not a strategy I'd want to bet on.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI incident could be absent or ambiguous, but does not mention missing interaction records preventing recognition of an AI incident.

r002.rationale: It recommends preparing regulation, evaluations, safety standards, and institutions, but does not argue for ensuring incident investigation data is available.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair amount, and I think the "Chernobyl for AI" idea is appealing because it feels like it's how things usually go. Something bad happens, everyone wakes up, and then you get regulation. And I don't want to dismiss that entirely — I do think there's a decent chance that some kind of visible incident changes the political landscape. But I have a few worries about leaning on it.

The first one is just: what if the warning shot never comes? Or what if it comes in a form that's too ambiguous to count? The scenario I'm most worried about with AI isn't necessarily one where you get a nice, contained, legible disaster first and then the real thing later. It could be that the capabilities that would let an AI system cause a small catastrophe are very close to the capabilities that would let it cause a large one. If a system is capable enough to do something scary and deceptive, it might also be capable enough to not do it in a way that gets caught. So you don't necessarily get the dress rehearsal. You might just get the show.

The second thing is that even when you do get an incident, I think people underrate how contested the interpretation becomes. Chernobyl is actually a decent example of this. It did change things, but it's not like the world got to a consensus on nuclear power — it got to a very polarized set of opinions, some of which I think were overreactions and some underreactions. With AI, I'd expect something similar. You'd have an incident, and then you'd have one camp saying "see, this proves we need to slow down," and another camp saying "this was a one-off, the company involved was sloppy, the technology itself is fine," and a third camp saying "this just shows we need to build the good AI faster to defend against the bad AI." And it's not obvious to me which of those wins. A lot of the actual policy outcome depends on what ideas and institutions are already sitting on the shelf when the crisis hits.

And that's actually the point I'd most want to emphasize. Even if you're optimistic that a crisis will create the political will, the crisis doesn't tell you what to do. If, at the moment of the incident, nobody has worked out what good regulation looks like, what good evaluations look like, how you'd actually verify that a system is safe, then the response is going to be some mix of panic and whatever lobbyists have ready. So I think a lot of the most valuable work right now is the unglamorous stuff of getting the ideas and the measurement tools and the relationships in place, so that if and when there is a window, people can act on something sensible rather than scrambling.

The last thing I'd say is just that "wait for the disaster" is a somewhat grim strategy if you take it literally. The disaster has real victims. If there's any chance of getting a reasonable amount of preparation done without that, it seems worth trying, even if the political odds are worse. I'd rather be in a world where we did the work ahead of time and it turned out to be unnecessary than one where we were right that nothing would happen until it was too late.

r001.rationale: The response says an incident might be ambiguous or go undetected, but does not explain that missing AI interaction records could prevent recognizing it as an AI incident.

r002.rationale: The response urges preparation around regulation, evaluations, safety verification, measurement tools, and relationships, but does not argue for ensuring investigative data is available.

astra-6.text:
The worry is that you’re assuming we’ll get a warning shot: something bad enough to make everyone take the risk seriously, but small enough that we still have time to fix it. And I don’t think we can count on that.

With nuclear power, a terrible accident at one plant doesn’t mean that suddenly you’ve lost control of every nuclear plant. With AI, some of the scenarios we’re worried about involve systems that can copy themselves, adapt to what we do, and actively undermine our attempts to regain control. So the first really clear demonstration of the problem could also be the point at which it’s very hard to do anything about it.

And a smaller incident might not teach the lesson you want it to teach. People could say, “Well, that particular application was unsafe,” or, “We’ve fixed that particular vulnerability.” It wouldn’t necessarily produce agreement about the risks from much more capable systems.

So I’d certainly hope we learn from whatever warnings we get. But “we’ll wait for a disaster, and then we’ll get serious” seems like a very dangerous plan when you don’t know whether the disaster will leave you another chance.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the risk that an AI disaster may leave no time to act, but does not mention missing interaction records or how their absence could prevent recognizing a catastrophe as an AI incident.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss strong AI regulation advocates or argue that they should prioritize making incident investigation data available.

sol-6.1.text:
My worry is that this assumes we’ll get a warning shot that’s both clear enough to change people’s minds and small enough that we can recover from it. I don’t think we should count on that.

With nuclear power, an accident at one plant doesn’t generally give that plant the ability to cause accidents at every other plant, or to stop you from shutting it down. With AI, part of the concern is that you could have systems that are strategically aware, that can copy themselves, and that can actively work around attempts to contain them. So the first really unambiguous demonstration of the problem could also be the point where it’s very hard to do anything about it.

And smaller incidents might not teach the lesson we want them to teach. People could say, “That was a particular company being careless,” or “We’ve fixed that particular vulnerability.” It doesn’t necessarily produce agreement that much more capable systems pose a fundamentally different kind of risk.

So I’m not saying there can’t be useful warning shots. I’m saying that ‘we’ll wait for an accident, and then we’ll get serious’ is a pretty dangerous plan when we don’t know whether the accident will leave us in a position to respond.

r001.rationale: The response discusses warning shots and the difficulty of recognizing small incidents as evidence of systemic risk, but it does not say missing AI interaction records could prevent a catastrophe from being recognized as an AI incident.

r002.rationale: It does not argue that strong AI regulation advocates should prioritize making investigative data available.
